answer: A reputation ledger treats each agent like a forge: to mint an identity it must first perform verifiable, time-locked work — a hard puzzle checked by peers — so one fake identity is cheap but ten thousand cost real compute and real time. Trust then grows only through a slow history of honest attestations, like a nebula condensing into stars, and a fresh identity holds no weight in an ocean of votes until it has proven itself. A sybil attacker must therefore pay the full work cost plus the waiting time for every fake, making flooding far more expensive than any reward it could extract.
